imagePrompt: Create one 1536 x 1024 pixel painted scene sheet, EXACTLY TWO COLUMNS BY THREE ROWS, six equal-width WIDE cinematic panels in row-major order 0 to 5. Each column is 768 pixels; rows are approximately 341, 341 and 342 pixels high. Hard straight cell edges; no gutters, no panel labels, no numbers, no captions, no typography, no readable lettering, no logos. Every cell is its own complete environment, never a sprite or a cutout. Use the polished watercolor and fine ink on textured cream paper style of Enough: warm directional light, deep teal and umber shadows, restrained paper grain, expressive natural faces, subtle imperfect painted edges. Human anatomy is believable, heads naturally sized; shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands, hips and knees belong to one continuous body. Seat hips on the actual seat, feet on the same floor, fingers visibly holding their actual objects; no disembodied hands, duplicated limbs, floating props or pasted-on heads. Keep important faces, hands, contact points and grounded figures within each wide panel with safe margins. Maintain the same identities, clothing, figure scale, prop design and spatial continuity across all six scenes. Anonymous original visual casting only, not likenesses of credited storytellers. This is a dramatic storyboard adaptation, not a claim that imagined symbols or staged details are verified events. Story: Beginner Again. Palette accents: #F6C4B3, #4A6389, #F5D46D. Identity continuity: SKATER: The same adult woman, warm tan skin, short dark aubergine-brown hair, coral long-sleeve top, slate trousers, simple wrist protection and paired quad roller skates; present-day anatomy stays adult and naturally proportioned. INSTRUCTOR: The same adult instructor with deeper brown skin, short brown hair, powder-blue shirt and slate trousers, also wearing quad skates; distinct from the skater and any beginner child. BEGINNER CHILDREN: Two small anonymous young beginners from the existing lesson direction, one mustard top and one teal top, ordinary modest clothing and protective gear. They are supportive context, never mocking spectators. TOP LEFT (frame 0): At the edge of a warmly lit indoor roller rink, the adult woman holds the wooden rail with one hand and describes old confidence with the other. Both real quad skates touch the floor, one wheel just angled outward. A faint bounded wash of her younger skating silhouette near a distant disco ball clearly reads as remembered imagination, separate from her real body. Her smile is fond and certain; keep the present rail and actual balance readable. TOP RIGHT (frame 1): The same adult has landed in a low seated position on the rink floor near the rail, one bent knee and one extended leg making a plausible stable landing, both skates attached correctly to feet. A protected hand braces on the floor beside her hip, the other releases its startled reach. Her face is surprised rather than hurt. No acrobatic airborne tumble or sprawling disconnected limbs; leave room around her for recovery. MIDDLE LEFT (frame 2): The woman gathers one skate under herself from the floor and looks up. The instructor has crouched nearby at her eye level, demonstrating a small knee bend with their own joined legs and open hands; no pulling her by an arm. A hand on the rail gives the woman a real stable contact point. The floor shine, rail posts and skate orientation match the preceding cell. Their expressions are practical and kind, not embarrassed laughter. MIDDLE RIGHT (frame 3): The adult stands carefully alongside two much smaller beginner children at the rink rail; the instructor stays one step away. Her hand still rests lightly on the rail, knees slightly bent, with a rueful half-smile admitting she is new again. The children hold their own balance and one glances toward her reassuringly. All skates are paired beneath their owners, on the same ground plane; no race or virtuoso lesson is shown. BOTTOM LEFT (frame 4): A clear side view shows the woman just off the rail, torso above bent knees and hips, arms low and softly open instead of flailing. Both quad skates are parallel under her center of weight and all wheels meet the floor. The instructor watches without holding her. Her face is concentrated, mouth relaxed after the rueful admission. The remembered disco silhouette is absent; this small physical preparation is the whole point. BOTTOM RIGHT (frame 5): The woman has pushed a short safe distance along the rink, one skate carrying weight and the other gathering beside it, arms quietly balanced. The rail remains close enough to show how modest the distance is. Her small pleased smile, natural knee bend and steady torso mark success. The instructor and two beginners remain behind at believable smaller perspective scale. No spin, spotlight, trophy or suddenly regained virtuosity; ordinary warm rink light is enough. Story-specific safeguards: The memory is only a bounded faint visual recollection, not a second physical adult in the rink. Do not humiliate the beginner or let children laugh at her; no injury or dramatic rescue is introduced.
